name: Acute Intermittent Porphyria

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and biochemical criteria for acute porphyrias

criteria.description: Markedly elevated urinary porphobilinogen (PBG) during acute attack (>10x upper limit of normal)
Reduced erythrocyte hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS) activity (~50% of normal)
Pathogenic variant identified in HMBS gene
Characteristic neurovisceral symptoms (abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric manifestations)
Dark or reddish-brown urine that darkens on standing
Normal fecal porphyrins (distinguishes from variegate porphyria and hereditary coproporphyria)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Elevated urinary PBG during symptomatic episode, confirmed by HMBS enzyme assay or HMBS genetic testing
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Up to 90% of individuals with HMBS mutations remain clinically latent. Attacks are typically provoked by drugs, hormones, fasting, or stress.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Severe colicky abdominal pain without peritoneal signs
pathognomonic.notes: Most common presenting symptom; pain is diffuse, poorly localized

pathognomonic.symptomName: Port wine or dark red-brown urine
pathognomonic.notes: Urine darkens upon standing due to PBG polymerization

occasional.notes: Predominantly motor; can progress to quadriparesis
Often due to hyponatremia from SIADH

rare.notes: Associated with chronic disease; long-term complication
Long-term risk in recurrent AIP; screening recommended after age 50

laboratory: Markedly elevated urinary porphobilinogen (PBG) during attack
Reduced erythrocyte HMBS enzyme activity (~50% of normal)
Normal fecal porphyrins (unlike HCP and VP)
imaging: Abdominal imaging typically unremarkable despite severe pain
MRI brain may show posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in severe cases
Hepatic MRI or ultrasound for HCC screening in chronic patients
other: Nerve conduction studies showing predominantly motor axonal neuropathy

distinguishingFeatures: HCP has elevated fecal coproporphyrin III
PCT presents with skin blistering, not neurovisceral attacks
PCT has elevated urinary uroporphyrins, not PBG
PCT does not cause abdominal pain attacks
Lead poisoning has elevated blood lead levels
ALA elevated but PBG normal in lead poisoning
Basophilic stippling on blood smear in lead poisoning
Imaging findings present in surgical abdomen
No autonomic dysfunction in typical surgical abdomen

redFlags: Progressive motor weakness suggesting ascending neuropathy (risk of respiratory failure)
references: Bissell DM, et al. Porphyria. N Engl J Med. 2017;377(9):862-872.
Anderson KE, et al. Recommendations for the diagnosis and treatment of the acute porphyrias. Ann Intern Med. 2005;142(6):439-50.
